reasoning: The statement joins cash handling, bookkeeping and banking. Cash work is partly live at a counter, partly hands-on counting, and banking is partly online and partly a trip to the bank. X separates these by type and place, as the physical/computer rule and Example D require. Y codes hands-on cash counting and deposits as DISCRETE desk work.

Filing electronic records is computer work, while copying, sorting and filing paper is hands-on, so the physical/computer rule calls for a split. Y does that. X also marks 832 as both a duplicate and an overlap, which is inconsistent; 832 covers wider system upkeep, so it is an overlap only.

Completing a bill, invoice or contract is computer work that produces a document. Stuffing, addressing and posting it is hands-on mail handling. X splits along that line as the instructions require; Y merges them into one DISCRETE batch.

Running copiers, scanners and fax machines is hands-on work at the machine, so it is PHYSICAL rather than DISCRETE as X codes it. Y separates the physical machine work from computer and voicemail use, which yields electronic items. Y's second part is broad, but its split follows the physical/computer rule.

Computing, recording and proofreading figures are steps toward one deliverable, an accurate record or report handed over as a whole. X codes that single unit; Y's split treats proofreading one's own entries as a separate handover, which it usually is not.

System upkeep is partly electronic and partly manual upkeep of paper files and lists, and the physical/computer rule calls for a split. Y does this. X wrongly marks 828 as a duplicate, when 828 is compiling and filing new records rather than keeping systems current.

Opening and routing incoming mail and preparing outgoing mail are hands-on, while answering correspondence produces written replies. X splits these three correctly by type. Y codes physical sorting as DISCRETE and lumps replies with posting.

A general office clerk often looks records up while a caller or visitor waits, and also works through written or queued requests. That is the Example D pattern of one activity done in two places, and Y splits on it. X treats it all as back-office work while admitting the live share in its notes.
Delivering messages and running errands are both PHYSICAL movement away from the desk with nothing to code further. Y's single part is sufficient, and X's split changes no coding outcome.

Taking inventory means physically counting supplies, while placing an order produces a purchase request the supplier and approver rely on. The physical/computer rule calls for a split, which X makes; Y folds the hands-on counting into a DISCRETE order.

A staff work schedule is a different deliverable from appointment bookings. Appointments are made both live and from written requests (Example D). X separates all three; Y lumps work schedules in with calendar update batches.

'Monitor' is an ongoing activity that step 3 says to recast into the items it produces. For a lead clerk those are reviews of subordinates' completed work, returned with corrections. X does this and keeps the direction as INTERPERSONAL; Y codes everything as INTERPERSONAL.

Troubleshooting office equipment is partly hands-on (cables, paper jams, toner) and partly computer-based diagnosis of software problems. The physical/computer rule calls for a split, which X makes; Y's single DISCRETE part hides the physical work it mentions in its notes.
